title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that compares a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and ran a shared initial generation (gpt-5-mini) per task. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 successful validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 across all pairs). We release the full preregistration, prompts, model/provider traces, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts. We interpret the result as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss implications for future evaluations that wish to demonstrate operational benefit from verifier/repair layers.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation promises efficiency gains in network operations but raises risk: incorrect or unsafe proposals can cause regressions. Prior literature advocates verifier‑assisted workflows (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) to reduce such risk by rejecting or repairing unsafe proposals before apply (e.g., generate‑validate‑repair pipelines and verifier‑based architectures). We designed a preregistered, paired experiment to quantify whether adding a verifier+repair layer reduces regression‑causing changes relative to accepting an LLM suggestion, holding the generator output fixed per task. The study was preregistered (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) and executed with full archival of prompts, responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: Recent work frames LLMs in NetOps as translators or assistants whose outputs must be validated by formal/symbolic verifiers or emulated checks. Benchmarks such as Cornetto evaluate generate→validate→repair pipelines at scale. Tool‑assisted self‑verification, grammar‑constrained decoding, and verifier‑guided agent architectures motivate our confirmatory design: measure the marginal operational value of inserting an automated verify/repair stage when the generator is fixed. We cite the closest prior evaluation artifacts for positioning (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: We preregistered a paired binary experiment (baseline vs guarded) with deterministic sampling of K=200 tasks from a public synthetic intent pool. Sampling and filtering rules, validator coverage requirements, and analysis code were frozen before execution. Key preregistered design choices: shared_initial_generation per task (independent_condition_generation=false), model requested = gpt-5-mini, one allowed repair attempt per guarded episode, maximum_model_calls=400, planned_episodes=400 (200 pairs). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (regression‑causing change rate difference). Primary test: exact McNemar (two‑sided) with bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Deterministic artifacts and logs were recorded for exact replay.
Implementation and artifacts (archived): all prompt texts, provider traces, shared initial responses, condition responses, and validator traces are archived under execution/ (see execution/execution_manifest.json). Model configuration is archived at execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). The deterministic validator identifier used for scoring is deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the preregistration constrained tasks to the validator’s covered features. Validator coverage and transformation metadata (allowed fields and the coverage matrix used to filter tasks) are archived at execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: 79c911558412d59f7fd9f4633b01a28cb8c3c7806c09dbf0b1f465650dc4d083). Representative task manifest entries (examples) show that allowed_fields = {"admin","mtu","vlan"} and that tasks were generated only when the validator reported coverage for the required features.
sections.results: Execution summary and primary outcome: The run completed as preregistered. Completed episodes = 400 (200 paired tasks); model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task). Primary outcome: baseline successful applies = 200/200 (1.0), guarded successful applies = 200/200 (1.0). Paired contingency: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Repair loop invocation: across the 200 guarded episodes the repair pathway was never applied (aggregate repair_applied = 0), as visible in the validator traces (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and others). Deterministic reconciliation checks passed (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json in the archive) and verify accounting consistency: planned_episodes=400, completed_episodes=400, model_calls_used=200, cache_miss/hit counts recorded, and no cross‑condition cache‑key reuse observed.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The preregistered hypothesis anticipated that adding a verifier/repair layer would reduce regression incidence relative to baseline. The observed null (no difference) arises because the shared initial generations were already validator‑compliant in every sampled case: the generator proposals met the validator constraints for all 200 tasks, so the verifier had no opportunity to block or request repair. Operational implication: when baseline generation attains very high validator compliance on the target distribution, the marginal safety value of an automatic verifier+repair layer (as implemented here) will be undetectable. This is a ceiling effect, not evidence that verifiers are never useful.
Required reviewer clarifications resolved from artifacts: (1) validator coverage — tasks were filtered to validator coverage; allowed_fields archived in execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: 79c911558412d59f7fd9f4633b01a28cb8c3c7806c09dbf0b1f465650dc4d083); per the manifest the validator supported the fields used in the tasks (admin, mtu, vlan). (2) preregistered power assumptions — the preregistration specified a target baseline failure rate = 0.20 and a target absolute reduction = 0.08 (alpha=0.05, power=0.80). The observed baseline success rate = 1.0 invalidates that power calculation: when observed baseline = 100%, the originally targeted detectable effect and sample‑size calculation are not applicable. We therefore interpret the confirmatory null as a design ceiling effect and recommend future confirmatory runs use (a) task pools with nontrivial baseline failure probability, (b) multiple generators or adversarially perturbed intents, or (c) higher‑fidelity emulation of operational regressions to expose verifier benefit.
Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): internal — shared_initial_generation was preregistered to be identical across arms (so the paired contrast isolates the verifier/repair effect); external — single model (gpt-5-mini) and deterministic synthetic tasks limit generalizability; construct — the primary outcome depends on the deterministic validator’s mapping from configuration to operational regression (validator fidelity recorded in execution/scoring/*.json). Reproducibility: full replay is possible from the archived manifests: execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/* (responses, provider_calls, scoring traces) with SHA‑256 manifests recorded.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation comparing a G→V→R pipeline to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline on a deterministic NetOps task pool. The observed result was a degenerate null: both arms produced validator‑compliant applies in all K=200 tasks (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p=1.00; bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]). This null is explained by a ceiling effect: the generator outputs already satisfied the deterministic validator for every sampled intent and thus the repair stage was never invoked. We release the complete preregistration, model/provider traces, responses, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. Future experimental designs seeking to demonstrate operational benefits of verifier/repair machinery should sample failure‑rich task distributions, include multiple generator models, or increase task realism and validator complexity.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 — external validity to production change intents is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator coverage and realism.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged items for this run.
